specsCards.title: 24-pin ATX
specsCards.detail:
• Main motherboard power connector
• Original ATX was 20-pin; modern is 24
• Carries +3.3V, +5V, +12V, standby
• Never force a mismatched plug

specsCards.title: CPU 8-pin (EPS)
specsCards.detail:
• Dedicated CPU power from the PSU
• 4-pin is older / lower TDP
• High-end boards may need dual 8-pin
• Undersized CPU power → instability

specsCards.title: PCIe power
specsCards.detail:
• 6-pin ≈ 75W extra
• 8-pin ≈ 150W extra
• Slot itself up to ~75W
• 12VHPWR on newer GPUs up to ~600W

specsCards.title: PSU sizing rule
specsCards.detail:
• Add GPU TDP + CPU TDP + ~50–100W
• Then add 20–30% headroom
• Example: 320W GPU + 125W CPU → 650W+
• Prefer quality 80 Plus units

specsCards.title: 80 Plus levels
specsCards.detail:
• Efficiency at 20% / 50% / 100% load
• Bronze < Silver < Gold < Platinum < Titanium
• Gold is a solid everyday target
• Higher tier ≠ always more watts

specsCards.title: SATA power
specsCards.detail:
• 15-pin drive power
• +3.3V orange (often unused)
• +5V red · +12V yellow
• Separate from 7-pin data

specsCards.title: Rail voltages
specsCards.detail:
• +12V feeds CPU and GPU (high current)
• Yellow = +12V · Red = +5V
• Orange = +3.3V · Black = ground
• Multimeter across yellow-black ≈ 12V

specsCards.title: Cat5e / Cat6 / Cat6a
specsCards.detail:
• Cat5e: 1 Gbps to 100 m
• Cat6: 10 Gbps ~55 m typical
• Cat6a: 10 Gbps to 100 m
• Prefer solid copper; avoid CCA for PoE

specsCards.title: Ethernet distance
specsCards.detail:
• Copper channel max 100 meters
• Includes patch cords in that total
• Beyond 100 m → fiber
• Applies to standard BASE-T runs

specsCards.title: Fiber types
specsCards.detail:
• Multimode: shorter campus runs
• Cheaper optics, LED/VCSEL sources
• Single-mode: long distance / ISP
• Kilometers-scale with lasers

specsCards.title: T568A vs T568B
specsCards.detail:
• Both are valid pinouts
• T568B common in the US
• Same standard both ends = straight-through
• A on one + B on other = crossover (rare now)

specsCards.title: USB power/data
specsCards.detail:
• USB 2.0: 480 Mbps, 5V/0.5A
• USB 3.x: 5 Gbps+ and more current
• USB-C may carry data + video + PD power
• Not every USB-C cable supports everything

specsCards.title: Plenum vs PVC
specsCards.detail:
• Plenum (CMP): air-handling spaces
• Low-smoke, fire-retardant jacket
• Riser (CMR): between floors
• Wrong jacket can fail inspection

specsCards.title: 2.4 vs 5 vs 6 GHz
specsCards.detail:
• 2.4 GHz: longest range, most interference
• Clean 2.4 channels: 1, 6, 11
• 5 GHz: more channels, less range
• 6 GHz (Wi-Fi 6E): clean, newest clients

specsCards.title: 802.11 generations
specsCards.detail:
• n = Wi-Fi 4 · ac = Wi-Fi 5
• ax = Wi-Fi 6 / 6E · be = Wi-Fi 7
• Exam still expects a/b/g/n/ac/ax awareness
• Know approximate capabilities

specsCards.title: WPA2 vs WPA3
specsCards.detail:
• WPA2-Personal: AES-CCMP + PSK
• WPA3-Personal: SAE, stronger offline resistance
• Prefer WPA3; WPA2 for legacy only
• Never use WEP

specsCards.title: SATA vs NVMe
specsCards.detail:
• SATA III cap ≈ 6 Gbps (~550 MB/s)
• NVMe Gen3 x4 ≈ 3.5 GB/s
• Gen4 x4 ≈ 7 GB/s
• Same M.2 slot may be SATA or PCIe

specsCards.title: M.2 sizes
specsCards.detail:
• Named WWLL: 2242, 2260, 2280, 22110
• 2280 is the common length
• Keying: B-key, M-key, B+M
• Must match the slot

specsCards.title: RAID quick math
specsCards.detail:
• RAID 0: capacity = sum, no safety
• RAID 1: capacity = one disk
• RAID 5: capacity = n−1, min 3 disks
• RAID 10: mirror + stripe, min 4

specsCards.title: RAM generations
specsCards.detail:
• DDR4 ≠ DDR5 (keying + voltage)
• Speeds are MT/s (e.g. DDR5-6000)
• Dual-channel: matched pairs, correct slots
• Usually slots 2 & 4 — check manual

specsCards.title: Well-known ports
specsCards.detail:
• 22 SSH · 23 Telnet · 25 SMTP
• 53 DNS · 67/68 DHCP
• 80 HTTP · 443 HTTPS
• 445 SMB · 3389 RDP · 389 LDAP

specsCards.title: TCP vs UDP choice
specsCards.detail:
• TCP: web, SSH, RDP, email
• UDP: VoIP, games, many DNS queries
• TCP when you need reliability
• UDP when latency matters most

specsCards.title: DHCP process
specsCards.detail:
• DORA: Discover → Offer → Request → Ack
• Server UDP/67 · Client UDP/68
• Failed DHCP → APIPA 169.254.x.x
• Reservations bind MAC to IP

specsCards.title: DNS records
specsCards.detail:
• A = IPv4 address
• AAAA = IPv6 address
• MX = mail server · CNAME = alias
• IP works, name fails → DNS

toolsItems.name: Crimper
toolsItems.desc:
• Attaches RJ-45 / RJ-11 plugs
• Essential for custom patch cables
• Pair with a good stripper
• Test after every crimp

toolsItems.name: Cable Stripper
toolsItems.desc:
• Removes outer jacket only
• Avoid nicking inner pairs
• Prep step before crimp/punchdown
• Different blades for cable types

toolsItems.name: Toner Probe
toolsItems.desc:
• Traces cables through walls/bundles
• Toner puts a signal on the wire
• Probe finds the tone
• Best for messy wiring closets

toolsItems.name: Cable Tester
toolsItems.desc:
• Verifies wire mapping
• Finds opens and shorts
• Some units measure length
• Use before blaming the switch

toolsItems.name: Punchdown Tool
toolsItems.desc:
• Seats wires into IDC blocks
• Patch panels and keystone jacks
• 110 and 66 blocks common
• Keep pairs untwisted only at the end

toolsItems.name: Loopback Plug
toolsItems.desc:
• Loops TX back to RX
• Tests NIC or switch port
• Handy when link light is dead
• Simple hardware isolation tool

toolsItems.name: Wi-Fi Analyzer
toolsItems.desc:
• Shows SSIDs and channels
• Signal strength + overlap
• Find cleaner channels
• Great for 2.4 GHz interference

toolsItems.name: Network Tap
toolsItems.desc:
• Copies traffic for monitoring
• Does not interrupt the link
• Used with analyzers/IDS
• Passive or active designs

toolsItems.name: Multimeter
toolsItems.desc:
• Measures voltage and resistance
• Continuity for fuses/cables
• Check PSU rails (yellow ≈ 12V)
• Basic electrical safety tool

toolsItems.name: POST Card
toolsItems.desc:
• Displays POST checkpoint codes
• Helps when there is no video/beeps
• PCIe, USB, or legacy ISA forms
• Match code to the BIOS list

visualItems.name: 24-pin ATX
visualItems.desc:
• Main motherboard power from the PSU
• +3.3V · +5V · +12V · grounds
• Seat until the latch clicks

visualItems.name: 8-pin CPU / EPS
visualItems.desc:
• Dedicated CPU power
• Often 4+4 split
• Required on modern boards

visualItems.name: PCIe 8-pin
visualItems.desc:
• GPU extra power ≈ 150W
• Cards may need one or more
• Match PSU cables to the card

visualItems.name: SATA Power
visualItems.desc:
• 15-pin drive power
• Separate from the data cable
• Color-coded voltage rails

visualItems.name: SATA Data
visualItems.desc:
• 7-pin data link
• HDD · SATA SSD · optical
• L-shaped keying

visualItems.name: RJ-45
visualItems.desc:
• Ethernet connector
• Eight conductors
• T568A or T568B termination

visualItems.name: HDMI
visualItems.desc:
• Digital video + audio
• Monitors · TVs · GPUs
• Not for networking

visualItems.name: DisplayPort
visualItems.desc:
• Digital video (PC common)
• Angled corner shape
• High-refresh friendly

visualItems.name: VGA
visualItems.desc:
• Legacy analog video
• Usually blue
• Prefer HDMI/DP when possible

visualItems.name: USB-C
visualItems.desc:
• Reversible connector
• Data ± video ± power
• Depends on cable + device

visualItems.name: LGA 1700
visualItems.desc:
• Intel 12th–14th gen desktop
• Pins in the board
• Align the CPU triangle marker

visualItems.name: AM5
visualItems.desc:
• AMD Ryzen 7000 / 9000
• Pins on the CPU — protect them
• Open the arm before seating

visualItems.name: M.2 NVMe
visualItems.desc:
• Compact SSD (often 2280)
• NVMe uses PCIe
• Confirm slot keying + type

visualItems.name: RAID 0
visualItems.desc: Striping only. No redundancy. Capacity = sum of disks. One failure = total loss.

visualItems.name: RAID 1
visualItems.desc: Mirroring. 100% redundant. Capacity = one disk. Survives one failure per pair.

visualItems.name: RAID 5
visualItems.desc: Stripe + distributed parity. Min 3 disks. Capacity = n-1. Survives one failure.

visualItems.name: RAID 10
visualItems.desc: Stripe of mirrors. Min 4 disks. High performance and redundancy.

flashcards.back:
• Main motherboard power
• Carries +3.3V, +5V, +12V, and grounds
• Seat until the latch clicks

• Dedicated processor power from the PSU
• Often split as 4+4
• Missing this cable → many builds will not POST

• 6-pin ≈ 75W extra to the GPU
• 8-pin ≈ 150W extra
• Slot can add up to ~75W more

• Powers SATA drives
• Separate from the 7-pin data cable
• Rails: +12V, +5V, +3.3V

• Data link for HDD / SATA SSD / optical
• L-shaped keying
• Keep runs tidy for airflow

• Intel socket for 12th–14th gen Core
• Lands on CPU, pins in the board
• Do not bend socket pins

• AMD socket for Ryzen 7000 / 9000
• Pins are on the CPU — protect them
• Open retention arm before seating

• Different notch, voltage, signaling
• Not interchangeable
• Use matched pairs for dual-channel

• NVMe uses PCIe (much faster)
• SATA SSDs share ~6 Gbps ceiling
• M.2 slots may be either — check the board

• RAID 0: stripe, no redundancy
• RAID 1: mirror, capacity of one disk
• RAID 5: stripe + parity, min 3 disks

• Eight-position Ethernet connector
• Terminate with T568A or T568B
• Match both ends for straight-through

• SSH — encrypted remote shell
• Also used for secure file transfer
• Prefer over Telnet (23)

• DNS — resolves names to IPs
• Uses UDP and TCP
• IPs work but names fail → suspect DNS

• DHCP server (67) and client (68)
• Automatic IP configuration
• Failure often yields APIPA 169.254.x.x

• HTTP (80) = unencrypted web
• HTTPS (443) = TLS encrypted
• Prefer 443 whenever possible

• RDP — Windows Remote Desktop
• Expose only with strong auth
• Prefer VPN in front when remote

• SMB — Windows file/printer sharing
• Sensitive on the public internet
• Common on local LANs

• Current preferred Wi-Fi security
• Uses SAE instead of older PSK handshake
• Stronger against offline attacks

• Improved efficiency and capacity
• Wi-Fi 6E adds 6 GHz
• Know 2.4 vs 5 vs 6 GHz tradeoffs

• 169.254.0.0/16 self-assigned range
• Appears when DHCP does not respond
• Means isolation or DHCP failure

• Two standard Ethernet pinouts
• Same standard on both ends = straight-through
• T568B is common in the US

• CMP-rated jacket for air-handling spaces
• Low-smoke materials
• Required by many fire codes in plenums

• Bare-metal virtualization
• Examples: ESXi, Hyper-V Server
• Runs on hardware without a host desktop OS

• Hosted virtualization
• Examples: Workstation, VirtualBox
• Runs on top of Windows / macOS / Linux

• IaaS: VMs, storage, networks
• PaaS: managed platform for apps
• SaaS: full software (email, Office online)

• Applies heat and pressure
• Bonds toner permanently to paper
• If toner smears off → suspect the fuser

• Holds the electrostatic image
• Defects often cause repeating marks
• Marks often match drum circumference

• Power over Ethernet
• DC power + data on one cable
• Used for APs, cameras, phones

• Power-On Self-Test at boot
• Firmware checks hardware before OS
• Beep / POST codes help isolate faults

• Measure voltage on PSU rails
• Yellow ~12V · Red ~5V
• Continuity mode finds broken wires/fuses

• Tone generator + inductive probe
• Traces a cable through walls
• Best for finding one cable in a bundle

• Seats conductors into IDC terminals
• Used on patch panels and keystone jacks

allQuestions.q: Which protocol is commonly used for contactless payments and short-range device pairing on smartphones?
allQuestions.e: NFC is designed for very short-range interactions such as payments and quick pairing.

allQuestions.q: A corporate phone will not join the office Wi-Fi that requires 802.1X. Home Wi-Fi works. What is the MOST likely missing piece?
allQuestions.e: Enterprise SSIDs usually need an EAP method and credentials pushed by MDM or configured manually.

allQuestions.q: A PC powers on, fans spin, but there are no beep codes and no video. Which tool helps isolate POST failures?
allQuestions.e: A POST diagnostic card can report codes when the system fails before video is available.

allQuestions.q: Intermittent random reboots under load with no BSOD. Temperatures are high. What is the BEST first action?
options: Clean dust, reseat cooler, verify thermal paste and fan curves
allQuestions.e: Thermal issues commonly cause reboots under load; cooling path is the first practical check.

allQuestions.q: One stick of RAM tested alone works in slot A but fails in slot B. What does this indicate?
options: The motherboard slot or channel is faulty
allQuestions.e: If the same module works in one slot and fails in another, the slot/channel is suspect.

allQuestions.q: A RAID 5 array with three disks reports one failed drive. Data is still accessible. What is the state?
options: Completely offline with total data loss
allQuestions.e: RAID 5 can survive one disk failure in a degraded state until the failed disk is replaced and rebuilt.

allQuestions.q: After replacing a failed disk in RAID 1, the array status shows 'rebuilding'. What does this mean?
options: Data is being copied to restore the mirror
The controller is erasing both disks
allQuestions.e: Rebuild copies data from the healthy mirror member onto the replacement disk.

allQuestions.q: S.M.A.R.T. reports increasing reallocated sectors on an HDD. What should the technician recommend?
allQuestions.e: Rising reallocated sectors are a classic early failure indicator; backup and replace.

allQuestions.q: A projector shows a faint image even when the input is correct and the lamp hours are low. Which is a common cause?
options: Dirty lens or clogged filters / failing lamp path
allQuestions.e: Projectors often dim due to dirty optics, blocked airflow, or aging lamp even before the rated hour limit.

allQuestions.q: Desktop video is fine on one monitor but a second DisplayPort monitor stays black. What should be checked FIRST?
options: Cable, input source selection, and GPU multi-monitor settings
Change the power supply wattage only
allQuestions.e: Second-display issues are most often cable, input selection, or multi-monitor configuration.

allQuestions.q: A phone overheats and throttles during normal use after a battery replacement with a third-party cell. What is MOST likely?
allQuestions.e: Aftermarket batteries with incorrect specs or poor thermal contact commonly cause heat and throttling.

allQuestions.q: A laptop intermittently disconnects from Wi-Fi when the lid angle changes. Wired Ethernet is stable. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Damaged antenna cable in the hinge path
allQuestions.e: Wi-Fi antenna wires run through the hinge; flex damage causes angle-dependent wireless dropouts.

allQuestions.q: Users report slow file transfers on a wired LAN. Link lights show 100 Mbps on a gigabit switch. What is a likely cause?
options: Bad cable / only two pairs negotiating, or duplex mismatch
allQuestions.e: 100 Mbps when gigabit is expected often means a damaged cable, wrong standard, or negotiation problem.

allQuestions.q: A workstation has IP 169.254.12.40 and cannot reach the internet. What is the FIRST service to verify?
allQuestions.e: APIPA means DHCP failed; check the DHCP path first.

allQuestions.q: A laser printer produces pages with a repeated mark every few inches. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Defective drum or roller with a fixed circumference defect
allQuestions.e: Repeating marks at a consistent interval usually match the circumference of a drum or roller.

allQuestions.q: Print jobs spool but never leave the queue on a networked printer. Other users can print. What should be checked on this PC FIRST?
options: Print spooler service, driver, and connectivity to the print queue
allQuestions.e: A single client that cannot print while others succeed points to local spooler, driver, or path issues.

allQuestions.q: Which RAID level provides striping with no parity or mirroring?
allQuestions.e: RAID 0 is pure striping with zero redundancy.

allQuestions.q: What is the minimum number of disks required for RAID 5?
allQuestions.e: RAID 5 needs at least three disks for data + distributed parity.

allQuestions.q: RAID 10 requires a minimum of how many disks?
allQuestions.e: RAID 10 is a stripe of mirrors and needs at least four disks.

allQuestions.q: Which tool injects a tone onto a cable so a probe can locate the other end in a bundle?
allQuestions.e: A tone generator and inductive probe (toner probe) are used to trace cables.

hardwareCards.title: CPUs & Sockets
hardwareCards.detail:
• LGA 1700 → Intel 12th–14th gen desktop
• AM5 → Ryzen 7000 / 9000 (pins on CPU — protect them)
• Match socket, cooler bracket, and BIOS support
• Check TDP vs cooler capacity before upgrading
• Update BIOS if the board shipped before the CPU existed

hardwareCards.title: Motherboards
hardwareCards.detail:
• Form factors: ATX, Micro-ATX, Mini-ITX (must fit case)
• Chipset sets CPU, RAM, PCIe, and storage limits
• Confirm M.2 keying: NVMe (M-key) vs SATA (B-key)
• Note fan headers, USB headers, and front-panel pins
• Standoffs must align — no shorting the board to the tray

hardwareCards.title: Memory (RAM)
hardwareCards.detail:
• DDR4 ≠ DDR5 — different notch, voltage, protocol
• Dual-channel: matched pairs in the correct slots (often 2nd & 4th)
• Speed = highest mutually supported by CPU + board + kit
• ECC mainly for servers/workstations
• Reseat and try one stick when diagnosing crashes

hardwareCards.title: Power Supplies
hardwareCards.detail:
• 24-pin board · 8-pin (or 4+4) CPU · PCIe 6/8 GPU
• Size: GPU TDP + CPU TDP + ~100W + 20–30% headroom
• Rails: Yellow +12V · Red +5V · Orange +3.3V · Black ground
• 80 Plus Bronze/Silver/Gold/Platinum/Titanium efficiency
• Modular cables reduce clutter; never force a connector

hardwareCards.title: Storage
hardwareCards.detail:
• SATA III ≈ 6 Gbps (~550 MB/s real-world ceiling)
• NVMe uses PCIe (Gen3/Gen4 x4 much faster)
• M.2 2280 most common; confirm slot type and length
• RAID 0 stripe (no safety) · RAID 1 mirror · RAID 5 parity (n−1)
• S.M.A.R.T. warnings → back up and replace soon

hardwareCards.title: GPUs & Expansion
hardwareCards.detail:
• Primary GPU in top PCIe x16 slot when possible
• 6-pin ≈ 75W · 8-pin ≈ 150W extra (plus ~75W from slot)
• Confirm case length, slot width, and PSU connectors
• Never force a card; check retention latch
• External display OK but internal black → cable/backlight

hardwareCards.title: Displays
hardwareCards.detail:
• IPS = color/angles · TN = cheap/fast · OLED = true black
• Note native resolution + refresh rate (Hz)
• HDMI and DisplayPort are digital; VGA is legacy analog
• Laptop: reseat display ribbons after screen work
• Dead pixels = panel; wrong colors = cable/profile/GPU

hardwareCards.title: Printers (laser)
hardwareCards.detail:
• Process: processing → charging → exposing → developing → transferring → fusing → cleaning
• Streaks/spots often → drum or toner
• Smear / toner rubs off → fuser
• Duplex-only jams → duplexer path
• Match PCL vs PostScript drivers to OS and apps

powerCards.title: 24-pin ATX
powerCards.detail:
• Main motherboard power from the PSU
• Carries +3.3V, +5V, +12V, 5VSB, and grounds
• Modern boards use 24-pin (older 20-pin exists)
• Seat until the retention latch clicks
• Never force a keyed connector the wrong way

powerCards.title: 8-pin CPU / EPS
powerCards.detail:
• Dedicated CPU power rail from the PSU
• Often split as 4+4 for flexibility
• High-end boards may need dual CPU power plugs
• Missing this → many systems will not POST
• Undersized CPU power → instability under load

powerCards.title: PCIe 6/8-pin
powerCards.detail:
• 6-pin ≈ 75W extra to the GPU
• 8-pin ≈ 150W extra
• PCIe slot itself can supply up to ~75W
• Use proper PSU cables; avoid weak adapters when possible
• Newer cards may use 12VHPWR / 12V-2x6

powerCards.title: SATA Power
powerCards.detail:
• 15-pin power connector for drives
• Separate from the 7-pin SATA data cable
• Rails include +12V, +5V, and +3.3V
• Orange +3.3V often unused by modern SSDs
• Daisy-chains common on non-modular PSUs

powerCards.title: Molex
powerCards.detail:
• Legacy 4-pin peripheral connector
• +5V (red) and +12V (yellow) with grounds
• Fans, pumps, older drives, adapters
• Not used for modern motherboard main power
• Still appears in adapter kits and cases

dataCards.title: SATA Data
dataCards.detail:
• 7-pin L-shaped data connector
• Used for HDD, SATA SSD, optical drives
• Hot-plug support depends on board/OS
• Keep cables tidy for airflow
• A failed cable can look like a failed drive

dataCards.title: USB family
dataCards.detail:
• Type-A host ports · Type-B on many printers
• USB-C reversible; may carry data + video + power
• USB 2.0 vs 3.x speeds differ sharply
• Not every USB-C cable supports all features
• Know minimum versions for your device needs

dataCards.title: HDMI
dataCards.detail:
• Digital video + audio on one cable
• Common on TVs, monitors, GPUs, laptops
• Not a network cable — do not confuse with Ethernet
• Versions affect max resolution/refresh
• Secure latch variants exist on some gear

dataCards.title: DisplayPort
dataCards.detail:
• Digital video common on PC GPUs
• Angled corner shape vs HDMI’s trapezoid
• Strong high-refresh and multi-stream support
• DP to HDMI adapters are common
• Check GPU output labels when “no signal”

dataCards.title: VGA
dataCards.detail:
• Legacy analog video (often blue connector)
• Prefer HDMI/DP for new installs
• Noise and blur more common on long runs
• Still appears on projectors and old displays
• Thumbscrews prevent accidental disconnect

dataCards.title: RJ-45 / RJ-11
dataCards.detail:
• RJ-45 = 8-conductor Ethernet
• RJ-11 = smaller phone connector
• Terminate Ethernet with T568A or T568B
• Same standard both ends = straight-through
• Crimp quality matters — test every cable

networkCards.title: Key ports
networkCards.detail:
• 22 SSH · 23 Telnet · 25 SMTP
• 53 DNS · 67/68 DHCP
• 80 HTTP · 443 HTTPS
• 110 POP3 · 143 IMAP · 389 LDAP
• 445 SMB · 3389 RDP
• Memorize these cold — they appear constantly

networkCards.title: TCP vs UDP
networkCards.detail:
• TCP = reliable, ordered, connection-oriented
• UDP = low latency, connectionless
• TCP: web, SSH, RDP, email
• UDP: VoIP, games, many DNS queries, streams
• Pick UDP when speed matters more than perfect delivery

networkCards.title: Wireless
networkCards.detail:
• 2.4 GHz: longer range, more interference (channels 1/6/11)
• 5 GHz: more channels, less range, less interference
• 6 GHz: Wi-Fi 6E — newest clients, cleaner spectrum
• Prefer WPA3-Personal; WPA2 for legacy only; never WEP
• Enterprise Wi-Fi often uses 802.1X / EAP

networkCards.title: SOHO router
networkCards.detail:
• Change default admin password immediately
• WPA3 + strong passphrase on Wi-Fi
• DHCP on correct LAN subnet; reservations for printers
• Guest network for visitors
• Port-forward only what you must; document rules

networkCards.title: Devices
networkCards.detail:
• Switch = MAC addresses / Layer 2
• Router = IP networks + broadcast domains / Layer 3
• Access point = wireless client access
• Firewall = allow/deny policy
• PoE = power + data for APs, cameras, phones
• ONT = fiber handoff from the ISP

networkCards.title: Cables & distance
networkCards.detail:
• Copper Ethernet channel: 100 meters max (includes patches)
• Cat5e: 1 Gbps to 100 m · Cat6: 10G ~55 m · Cat6a: 10G to 100 m
• T568B common in the US — match both ends for straight-through
• Plenum (CMP) jacket in air-handling spaces
• Beyond 100 m copper → use fiber

networkCards.title: IP & DNS
networkCards.detail:
• DHCP DORA: Discover → Offer → Request → Ack
• DHCP fail → APIPA 169.254.x.x (isolated)
• A = IPv4 · AAAA = IPv6 · MX = mail · CNAME = alias
• IP works but name fails → DNS problem
• Gateway wrong → no path off the LAN

networkCards.title: Tools
networkCards.detail:
• Crimper → RJ-45/RJ-11 ends on patch cables
• Punchdown → patch panels and keystone jacks
• Cable tester → wire map, opens, shorts
• Toner probe → trace a cable through walls
• Loopback → test NIC or switch port hardware
• Wi-Fi analyzer → channels, overlap, signal

mobileCards.title: Hardware replace
mobileCards.detail:
• Common FRUs: battery, display, storage, Wi-Fi card, keyboard
• Disconnect or isolate battery before internal work
• After screen jobs: reseat every display ribbon
• Touch dead but external OK → digitizer or cable
• Swollen battery → stop using, replace safely, do not puncture

mobileCards.title: Connectors & docks
mobileCards.detail:
• USB-C may carry data, video, and power — depends on cable + device
• Thunderbolt docks: multi-display + high bandwidth
• NFC: short-range payments and pairing
• Bluetooth: headsets, keyboards, mice
• Not every USB-C cable supports video or full Power Delivery

mobileCards.title: Cellular & hotspot
mobileCards.detail:
• Physical SIM and/or eSIM profiles
• Hotspot shares cellular data to other devices
• Clients online but no internet → check cellular data/cap/APN
• Airplane mode disables radios (you can re-enable Wi-Fi)
• Roaming and data caps cause “mysterious” outages

mobileCards.title: Mobile networking
mobileCards.detail:
• Enterprise Wi-Fi often needs 802.1X / EAP credentials
• MDM pushes Wi-Fi, VPN, email, and security profiles
• VPN protects traffic on open networks
• IMAP vs POP3: IMAP keeps mail on server; POP often downloads off
• Know when to reset network settings vs replace hardware

mobileCards.title: Symptoms & safety
mobileCards.detail:
• Ghost touch → digitizer or screen assembly
• No charge → try known-good cable and brick first
• Liquid damage → power off, inspect for corrosion
• Overheating → check apps, case, battery health
• Always use ESD-safe practices on internal repairs

cloudCards.title: Type 1 hypervisor
cloudCards.detail:
• Bare-metal: runs on hardware (no host desktop OS)
• Examples: VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V Server, Xen
• Datacenter standard for performance and isolation
• Manages CPU, RAM, storage, and network for VMs

cloudCards.title: Type 2 hypervisor
cloudCards.detail:
• Hosted on top of a full OS (Windows, macOS, Linux)
• Examples: VMware Workstation, VirtualBox, Parallels
• Great for labs and desktops; slightly more overhead
• Host OS failure can take guests down

cloudCards.title: VDI
cloudCards.detail:
• Virtual Desktop Infrastructure — desktops run in the datacenter
• Streamed to thin or thick clients
• Broker/hosts down → thin clients show nothing useful
• Centralizes updates, security, and backups

cloudCards.title: IaaS
cloudCards.detail:
• Infrastructure as a Service: VMs, storage, virtual networks
• You manage OS, middleware, and apps
• Provider manages hardware and virtualization fabric
• Example mindset: “I rent the machines”

cloudCards.title: PaaS
cloudCards.detail:
• Platform as a Service: managed runtime and tools
• Deploy apps without babysitting servers
• Provider handles OS and much of the stack
• Example mindset: “I deploy the app”

cloudCards.title: SaaS
cloudCards.detail:
• Software as a Service: full apps (email, Office, CRM)
• Browser or light client — provider manages almost everything
• Example mindset: “I just log in”
• Patching and uptime largely the vendor’s job

cloudCards.title: Cloud traits
cloudCards.detail:
• Rapid elasticity — scale out/in with demand
• Measured service — metered billing
• Resource pooling — multi-tenant hardware
• Broad network access — reach services over the network
• On-demand self-service — provision without tickets

troubleCards.title: POST & no boot
troubleCards.detail:
• POST checks hardware before the OS loads
• Beeps / POST codes → RAM, video, CPU, board
• Fans spin, no video → reseat RAM and GPU first
• Burning smell or smoke → power off immediately
• Clear CMOS if settings or overclock went wrong

troubleCards.title: RAM & CPU
troubleCards.detail:
• Random crashes under load → memory or thermals
• Try one stick at a time; reseat firmly
• Check cooler mount, thermal paste, and dust
• CPU overheat → throttle or shutdown
• Memtest-style tools help confirm bad RAM

troubleCards.title: Drives & RAID
troubleCards.detail:
• Clicking HDD → back up now, replace drive
• S.M.A.R.T. warning → plan replacement before failure
• RAID 0: one disk fails = all data gone
• RAID 5: replace failed disk and rebuild ASAP
• Loose SATA power/data cables mimic “dead drive”

troubleCards.title: Video & displays
troubleCards.detail:
• External OK, internal black → cable, inverter, or backlight
• Fuzzy projector → focus, input source, resolution
• Dead pixels → panel replacement
• Wrong colors → cable, color profile, GPU
• No signal → input selection, cable, GPU output

troubleCards.title: Network symptoms
troubleCards.detail:
• 169.254.x.x → DHCP failed (APIPA)
• No link light → cable, NIC, or switch port
• Wi-Fi drops near microwave → 2.4 GHz interference
• Port flapping → bad cable or bad port
• IP works, names fail → DNS

troubleCards.title: Printer defects
troubleCards.detail:
• Streaks / repeating marks → drum or toner
• Smear / rubs off → fuser not bonding toner
• Duplex-only jam → duplexer path
• Inkjet bands → clean nozzles / check heads
• Wrong driver (PCL vs PS) causes garbage output

troubleCards.title: Mobile issues
troubleCards.detail:
• Swollen battery → replace; do not crush or puncture
• Ghost touches → digitizer/screen assembly
• After screen swap → reseat ribbons before replacing parts again
• Slow charge → known-good cable and adapter first
• Overheat + shutdown → battery or thermal path

troubleCards.title: Methodology
troubleCards.detail:
1. Identify the problem
2. Establish a theory of probable cause
3. Test the theory
4. Establish a plan of action and implement
5. Verify full functionality
6. Document findings
• Change one variable at a time

memoryCards.title: 22 SSH
memoryCards.detail:
• You're 22 — get a secure shell
• SSH = encrypted remote login
• Prefer over Telnet (23)

memoryCards.title: 53 DNS
memoryCards.detail:
• 5-3: name to IP
• DNS resolves hostnames
• IP works, name fails → DNS

memoryCards.title: 67 / 68 DHCP
memoryCards.detail:
• 67 offers, 68 takes the lease
• Server 67 · Client 68
• Fail → APIPA 169.254.x.x

memoryCards.title: 80 vs 443
memoryCards.detail:
• 80 open road · 443 locked gate
• HTTP cleartext vs HTTPS TLS
• Always prefer 443

memoryCards.title: 3389 RDP
memoryCards.detail:
• 33-89 remote desktop please
• Windows Remote Desktop
• Use strong auth / VPN

memoryCards.title: 445 SMB
memoryCards.detail:
• 4-4-5 share the drive
• Windows file & printer sharing
• Don't expose to the internet

• 25 Send Mail · 110 POP off · 143 IMAP stays
• SMTP send · POP download · IMAP sync
• Know when mail leaves the server

memoryCards.title: Wire colors
memoryCards.detail:
• Yellow 12 · Red 5 · Orange 3.3 · Black ground
• +12V feeds CPU/GPU
• Multimeter: yellow to black ≈ 12V

memoryCards.title: PCIe watts
memoryCards.detail:
• 6-pin ≈ 75W · 8-pin ≈ 150W
• Slot can add ~75W more
• Match cables to the card

memoryCards.title: PSU sizing
memoryCards.detail:
• GPU + CPU + ~100W, then +20–30%
• Headroom prevents shutdowns
• Quality > paper watts

memoryCards.title: Main connectors
memoryCards.detail:
• 24-pin board · 8-pin CPU · PCIe GPU
• Missing CPU power → no POST
• Latch must click

memoryCards.title: RAID 0 / 1 / 5
memoryCards.detail:
• 0 = zero safety · 1 = mirror · 5 = parity
• RAID 5 needs 3+ drives
• RAID 0: one disk dies = all gone

memoryCards.title: SATA vs NVMe
memoryCards.detail:
• SATA = seatbelt · NVMe = rocket
• SATA ~6 Gbps ceiling
• M.2 slot may be either — check manual

memoryCards.title: DDR4 vs DDR5
memoryCards.detail:
• Different notch — they don't mix
• Matched pairs for dual-channel
• Speed = highest mutual support

memoryCards.title: 2.4 GHz channels
memoryCards.detail:
• 1-6-11 stay alive
• Only non-overlapping set in the US
• Microwaves thrash 2.4 GHz

memoryCards.title: 100 meter rule
memoryCards.detail:
• 100 steps then go fiber
• Copper Ethernet channel max
• Includes patch cords

memoryCards.title: T568B
memoryCards.detail:
• B is common in the US
• Same standard both ends = straight-through
• Don't mix A and B by accident

memoryCards.title: DHCP DORA
memoryCards.detail:
• DORA explores for an IP
• Discover → Offer → Request → Ack
• Always that order

memoryCards.title: OSI pizza
memoryCards.detail:
• Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away
• Physical → Data Link → Network → Transport → Session → Presentation → Application
• Switch L2 · Router L3

memoryCards.title: Methodology
memoryCards.detail:
• I Think The Puppy Is Very Delightful
• Identify → Theory → Test → Plan → Implement → Verify → Document
• One change at a time

memoryCards.title: APIPA
memoryCards.detail:
• 169.254 means I'm alone
• DHCP did not answer
• Check cable, VLAN, DHCP server

memoryCards.title: Printer defects
memoryCards.detail:
• Streaks drum · smear fuser · duplex jam duplexer
• Toner rubs off → fuser
• Duplex-only problem → duplexer

memoryCards.title: POST beeps
memoryCards.detail:
• Beeps before OS = hardware talking
• No video → listen or use POST card
• Burning smell → power off first

memoryCards.title: IaaS PaaS SaaS
memoryCards.detail:
• IaaS rent machines · PaaS deploy app · SaaS just log in
• Pizza: toppings vs delivered pie
• Know who manages what

memoryCards.title: Type 1 vs 2
memoryCards.detail:
• Type 1 touches the floor (bare metal)
• Type 2 rides on an OS
• ESXi/Hyper-V vs Workstation/VirtualBox

memoryCards.title: Port song
memoryCards.detail:
• 22 · 53 · 67/68 · 80/443 · 445 · 3389
• SSH DNS DHCP Web SMB RDP
• Sing until automatic

portsCards.detail:
• FTP data (20) and control (21)
• Unencrypted file transfer
• Prefer SFTP/SSH when possible

• SSH — secure remote shell
• Encrypted management + file transfer
• Prefer over Telnet

• Telnet — remote terminal
• Unencrypted (avoid on open networks)
• Legacy only

• SMTP — send email between servers
• Often filtered on residential ISPs
• Submission often uses 587

• DNS — name resolution
• UDP and TCP
• IPs work, names fail → DNS

• DHCP — server 67, client 68
• Automatic IP configuration
• Failure → APIPA 169.254.x.x

• HTTP — unencrypted web
• Cleartext traffic
• Prefer HTTPS 443

• POP3 — download email to client
• Often removes mail from server
• Legacy in many orgs

• IMAP — email stays on server
• Multi-device friendly
• Common for modern mail

• LDAP — directory queries
• Auth and directory lookups
• LDAPS uses 636

• HTTPS — encrypted web (TLS)
• Default for secure sites
• Memorize this one cold

• SMB / CIFS — Windows file sharing
• Printer sharing too
• Do not expose to the open internet

• RDP — Remote Desktop
• Windows remote GUI
• Lock down with strong auth / VPN

• NetBIOS / NetBT
• Legacy Windows name services
• Still seen on some LANs
